> 大道氾兮，其可左右。萬物恃之而生而不辭，功成不名有.

For fourteen chapters the camera has been on people: how to stop forcing, stop relying on force, stop grasping names, stop competing outward.

Chapter 34 turns it around for the first time and asks: what does the Dao itself do?

The answer is two characters: 不主 — it does not act as master.

## 做主 and 不主

People chase 大, and what they mean by it is mastery: to command, to unify, to bring everything into one order. To gather what belongs to others into my arrangement.

The Dao's 大 is the opposite: to carry, to circulate, to nourish, to let be. To let what belongs to you remain yours.

One thing, two directions. 做主 is 合. 不主 is 和.

Which is why this chapter is not just another chapter: it is the ballast under the whole 和/合 line. The previous fourteen proved people should not force unity. This one proves the Dao never forced it to begin with.

A rule and a ground. The rule is not painful because the ground was always like this.

## 氾 and 左右

氾 — flooding, spreading without a center. Not "the Dao is everywhere" as a slogan, but: there is no point from which it is administered.

其可左右 — it can go left or right. It does not take one side and hold it. This is the structural reason it can be 不主: a thing that has chosen a side must defend that side, and defending is mastery.

## 不辭, 不名有, 不為主

萬物恃之而生而不辭 — everything relies on it to live, and it does not refuse. 辭 is to decline, to refuse the burden. The Dao does not audit who deserves to be sustained.

功成不名有 — the work is accomplished and it does not take the name of owner. 名有 is to have one's name registered on the achievement. In the administrative language of the period, 功 is recorded and 名 is claimed — two separate acts. The Dao completes the first and declines the second.

衣養萬物而不為主 — it clothes and feeds everything and is not their master.

## 小 and 大

> 常無欲，可名於小；萬物歸焉而不為主，可名為大.

Two measures, one thing.

No craving, therefore it can be called 小 — small as in having no scale of its own, no claim that requires space.

Everything returns to it and it does not act as master, therefore it can be called 大 — great as in having no boundary.

Note that both names come from the same fact: 不為主. It is small because it takes no position, and great because nothing is excluded from it.

## 以其終不自為大，故能成其大

Because it never makes itself great, it can complete its greatness.

This is the sentence the chapter exists to deliver, and it is not a paradox. Greatness that has to be maintained has a maintenance cost, and the cost is drawn from the same capacity. Greatness that does not require maintenance has the whole capacity available.

## What changes if you accept this

The previous chapters were instructions. This one is a description of how the thing being imitated actually behaves.

That matters for the reason instructions usually fail: a rule you follow because you were told to is a position you have to defend. A behavior you adopt because it is how the structure works requires no defense — it is simply what you do when you understand the structure.
